title: Bandwidth & Bottleneck Estimation
summary: Turning requests and payload size into Mbps/Gbps, and figuring out which resource — compute, storage, or network — actually binds the design before you scale the wrong one.

slides.markdown:
QPS and storage estimates tell you how much work a system does; bandwidth tells you whether the pipes can carry it. This topic converts request volume and payload size into network capacity, then asks the question that actually decides what to scale: is this system CPU-bound, storage-bound, or network-bound?

Getting the answer wrong means scaling the wrong tier while the real bottleneck — often the network link, not the servers — stays maxed out.

slides.sectionTitle: Bandwidth math: requests x payload size -> Mbps/Gbps
slides.markdown:
Bandwidth is QPS times payload size, with one unit trap: network capacity is quoted in **bits**, but payload sizes are almost always in **bytes** — you must multiply by 8.

```
10,000 QPS x 50 KB response payload

Bytes/sec = 10,000 x 50,000 bytes        = 500,000,000 B/s
                                          = 500 MB/s

Bits/sec  = 500,000,000 B/s x 8          = 4,000,000,000 bit/s
                                          = 4 Gbps
```

Forgetting the x8 byte-to-bit conversion is the single most common error in bandwidth estimates — it silently understates the number you need by 8x.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: where bandwidth limits actually bite (client, LB, DB)
slides.markdown:
![A request path pipe from client to DB narrowing at three pinch points: last-mile link, load balancer NIC, and inter-node replication link](assets/bandwidth-pinch-points.svg)

Bandwidth limits rarely bite where people first look. A single client's last-mile connection is almost never your bottleneck — but the load balancer's network interface has a fixed cap (often 10-25 Gbps per instance), and every request funnels through it. Database nodes have their own limit too: replication traffic between them can saturate an internal link long before any client-facing number looks alarming.

Check all three points separately — the tightest one, not the average, sets your ceiling.

slides.sectionTitle: Identifying the binding constraint: compute vs storage vs network
slides.markdown:
Every system has exactly one resource that saturates first under load, and it's rarely the one intuition points to. **Compute-bound** systems max out CPU or GPU cycles — think video transcoding or ML inference. **Storage-bound** systems max out disk IOPS or throughput — think a database serving heavy random reads. **Network-bound** systems max out link bandwidth — think video streaming or large file transfer.

Estimate all three independently (CPU-seconds per request, disk IOPS per request, bytes per request) rather than assuming the app tier is always the constraint.

The binding resource is whichever one hits its ceiling first under your actual traffic — scale that one, and only that one, first.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: video streaming bandwidth estimate
slides.markdown:
Assumptions: 1 million concurrent viewers, each streaming at a typical 1080p adaptive bitrate of 3 Mbps.

```
Total bandwidth = 1,000,000 viewers x 3 Mbps
                = 3,000,000 Mbps
                = 3,000 Gbps
                = 3 Tbps
```

No single datacenter's uplink carries 3 Tbps to end users directly — this is exactly why video platforms push content to CDN edge nodes close to viewers instead of serving every stream from one origin. The bandwidth number, not the CPU or storage number, is what forces that architectural decision.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: CPU-bound vs I/O-bound vs network-bound systems
slides.markdown:
| | CPU-bound | I/O-bound (storage) | Network-bound |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example workload | video transcoding, ML inference | OLTP database, random reads | video streaming, large file transfer |
| Bottleneck resource | CPU/GPU cycles | disk IOPS/throughput | NIC or link bandwidth |
| Typical fix | scale out, or offload to GPU | faster disks (NVMe), caching, more IOPS | CDN, edge caching, bigger links |

**How to decide:** load-test and watch utilization on all three — CPU, disk IOPS, network egress — under realistic traffic. Whichever hits 100% first is the real constraint, regardless of which one you assumed going in.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: estimating servers needed without checking network egress cost
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I sized enough app servers to handle the CPU load, so the server count is the whole answer."

**Why it's wrong:** a CPU-based server count says nothing about whether the network can physically carry that traffic. A single mid-sized cloud instance's network interface is commonly capped somewhere in the 5-10 Gbps range — a workload needing terabits of egress, like video streaming, needs orders of magnitude more egress-capable capacity (or a CDN) than CPU sizing alone would suggest, and egress is also billed separately from compute.

**Correct model:** size network egress bandwidth as its own line item, independent of CPU and storage — it has its own ceiling and its own cost, and it can be the actual binding constraint even when compute looks fine.
